title: scheduling-queue-freeze-cni-flap-playbook-wip
content:
Summary:
Observed a hard freeze of the kube-scheduler scheduling queue after a CNI dataplane flap in us-west-2 causing podPending spikes across two node pools. Symptoms included: scheduled pods not binding for 40–90s, large kube-scheduler latency p95 and p99, sustained node pressure on CPU and net-dev rx/tx queues, and CNI heartbeats failing to update IPAM state. This doc is working notes + an operational playbook for triage and short-term mitigations; does not attempt a full postmortem root cause — that's a follow-up.

High level timeline (rough):
- 2025-01-11 03:17 UTC: first alert — k8s API write latencies increased, some control-plane traces showing scheduler queue depth increased to ~8k.
- 03:19 UTC: spike in pod Pending counts + autoscaler activity observed (scale-up of node-pool-a started).
- 03:20–03:25 UTC: SRE oncall saw CNI dataplane errors from node-exporter logs: kernel tx queue drops, cni-plugin restarted on ~60 nodes.
- 03:26 UTC: k8s scheduler leader logged consecutive scheduling attempts timing out at 30s; backlog grew.
- 03:40 UTC: manual mitigation: cordon + drain of most impacted nodes + fallback to alternate CNI config on a small canary pool.
- 04:05 UTC: backlog subsided gradually as CNI served stable heartbeats; scheduler latency returned to baseline ~04:12 UTC.

Key observations / metrics collected:
- scheduler_queue_depth p99 ~ 8k at peak (baseline < 50)
- scheduler_bind_latency p95 ~ 45s during incident (baseline < 200ms)
- node CPU steal on impacted nodes increased by +20% during kernel tx queue backlog
- kernel tx/rx queue drops correlated with spikes in egress NAT retransmits (per node netstat)
- cni-plugin restarts: ~3 restarts/node where observed
- kubelet eviction threshold hit on ~12 nodes due to ephemeral-fd exhaustion (file descriptor growth tied to conntrack table increases)

Hypothesis (short):
A transient external egress traffic surge (customer load + canary traffic) caused NAT/conntrack table growth. The host kernel began dropping packets on netdev queues, which caused the CNI dataplane to fail probes and restart. Restarts caused ephemeral IP state to be stale, kube-proxy rules TTL churn increased, and scheduler started piling pods because kubelet/node readiness flapped and node conditions reported NETWORK_UNAVAILABLE briefly. Secondary effects: autoscaler scaled up nodes into a partially degraded network state which worsened control plane latencies.

Immediate mitigations applied during incident (what worked):
- Rapid cordon of the top 10 most saturated nodes (kubectl cordon) to stop new pods landing on them.
- Selective drain of pods that were sensitive to network (stateful services) to reduce conntrack load.
- Temporarily increased conntrack max on impacted nodes via sysctl (net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max) with a later plan to tune properly.
- Flushed conntrack on a canary node to validate recovery (conntrack -F) — WARNING: stateful traffic disruption.
- Rolled back a recent CNI plugin auto-update applied ~02:55 UTC to the stable image on a small canary pool — this eliminated a regression vector.
- Throttled the egress layer for a noisy customer prefix at the edge LB for 30 minutes (rate-limit) which visibly reduced kernel queue drops.

Short-term playbook / triage checklist (first 10–30 minutes):
1) Identify scope quickly:
   - kubectl get cs, nodes --no-headers | awk '{print $1, $2, $3}'
   - kubectl get pods --all-namespaces -o wide | grep Pending | wc -l
   - Check scheduler metrics: prometheus query scheduler_queue_depth, scheduler_binding_latency
2) Look at node dataplane health:
   - ssh to impacted node(s), run: sudo ss -s; sudo cat /proc/net/softnet_stat; dmesg | tail -n 100
   - sysctl net.core.netdev_max_backlog; ip -s link show dev eth0 (or the CNI iface)
   - sudo conntrack -L | head -n 80; sudo cat /proc/sys/net/netfilter/nf_conntrack_count
3) CNI/plugin checks:
   - kubectl -n kube-system get pods -l app=cni -o wide; kubectl logs <cni-pod> --since=15m
   - check cni-plugin health endpoint (if present) e.g curl http://127.0.0.1:15020/health on node
4) Scheduler & API server checks:
   - kubectl -n kube-system logs -l component=kube-scheduler --tail=200
   - kubectl get events --sort-by='.lastTimestamp' | tail -n 100
5) If conntrack exhaustion suspected, do this in safe, measured way:
   - Increase nf_conntrack_max by +30% on one canary node and monitor: sudo sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=210000
   - Avoid blanket conntrack flush unless you can tolerate session drops. If you must, pick a canary node and run sudo conntrack -F and observe application impact.
6) Node cordon/drain pattern:
   - kubectl cordon <node>
   - kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=60 --timeout=10m
   - If drain hangs due to network attach/detach, consider --force and be prepared to restart kubelet after scheduling finishes.
7) Autoscaler & rollout controls:
   - Pause Cluster Autoscaler scaling to avoid adding degraded nodes: annotate cluster-autoscaler: spec.paused=true (internal guide link)
   - If a CNI rollout was recently applied, rollback to previous image on a canary subset.

Commands and snippets used during triage (notes/logs):
- prometheus:q: sum(rate(kube_scheduler_schedule_attempts_total[1m])) by (result)
- kubectl get nodes -o json | jq '.items[] | {name:.metadata.name, conditions:.status.conditions}'
- sudo cat /proc/net/softnet_stat | awk '{print $1, $4, $5}' # watch for dropped packets
- sudo ss -tuna | wc -l  # socket count to detect fd growth
- sudo sysctl -w net.netfilter.nf_conntrack_max=210000
- sudo conntrack -F  (used on canary only)

Open questions / follow-ups (to turn into postmortem RCA workstreams):
- Why did kernel netdev queues become saturated — was traffic amplification coming from within cluster or external ingress? Need flow records from edge LBs.
- What CNI change was rolled out before incident and could it have altered conntrack handling? Audit the image build CI and the canary rollout timeline.
- Why did autoscaler decide to scale when network signals suggested degraded capacity? Should autoscaler consider node network readiness metrics before scaling?
- Are our default conntrack_max and netdev_max_backlog sensible for current customer traffic patterns? Create a capacity model.
- Can we add a lightweight UDP/TCP dataplane probe per node to surface kernel tx/rx queue health into monitoring?

Longer-term mitigations / follow-ups (owner assignments to propose in postmortem):
- eng-sre: Implement a per-node netdev/conntrack synthetic probe and add alerting when nf_conntrack_count > 70% of nf_conntrack_max.
- infra-networking: Evaluate moving noisy egress prefixes to a separate egress NAT gateway to avoid host conntrack pressure.
- platform: Temporarily add a scheduler predicate to deprioritize nodes with recent CNI restarts or netdev drop signals (pilot in canary cluster).
- deploy: Harden CNI rollout playbook: staged rollout with active probe validation, rollback after X restarts within 15m.
- cost/ops: Run a traffic audit for the hours prior to the incident to identify customer(s) that triggered spike; consider quota/traffic-shaping policies.

Notes to self (informal):
- avoid mass conntrack flushes except as last resort; do canary + observe.
- we should keep a quick script for cordon+drain+label and a template Slack message for affected services.
- watch out for noisy L7 retries that can amplify egress connections — consider increasing client-side keepalive to reduce new sockets.

Appendix: short playbook stub to convert to a formal runbook:
- Detect: metrics rule -> scheduler_queue_depth > 200 && nf_conntrack_count > 80% -> P1
- Triage: assess whether CNI restarts correlated; check netdev queue drops and conntrack growth
- Contain: cordon top saturated nodes, throttle noisy egress prefixes, pause autoscaler, rollback CNI if new
- Remediate: increase conntrack_max on affected nodes (canary), drain worst nodes, fix CNI images/configs
- Recovery: uncordon nodes gradually, resume autoscaler when net metrics stable for 10m
- Postmortem: collect flows, CNI rollout logs, autoscaler decision logs, kubelet logs + kernel ring buffer

If you are oncall and reading this: prioritize containment first (cordon + throttle) and call network-eng immediately if egress shaping is needed. Add any missing steps or command snippets here and I'll fold them into the next draft.

-- Anika (oncall)
__notes: Informal, iterative draft — intended to be converted into a formal runbook after RCA. Keep this doc in drive for quick access during future similar incidents.
